The Buddha said pain in life is inevitable. Suffering is optional.

Kevin Trudeau's example: kids who beg to go to the haunted house, screaming and laughing at the same time on a roller coaster, women walking out of a sad movie in tears calling it the best movie they'd ever seen.

None of that is suffering. It's pain you're choosing to feel, as a witness to your life instead of a victim of it.

You can feel everything fully and still never suffer.

Kevin Trudeau had dozens of cars worth millions and homes in Zurich, Sydney, New York, Chicago, Dallas, Florida, Beverly Hills and Ojai, some staffed and furnished with fine art, all at once.

Then the government took it all away.

People asked how he was coping. He says he felt nothing, because he was never attached to any of it. He'd enjoyed it while it was his. Now it's somebody else's turn.

When you're not attached to something, losing it doesn't touch you.

A man on a hoarding show had a shoebox of old, bent bottle caps. Not his. No sentimental value. Worth nothing, not even as scrap.

The producers picked it as the easiest thing to remove — something small to start with.

He started shaking. "I can't let those go. I just can't."

Kevin Trudeau's point: that's not really about bottle caps. His energy had attached itself to them, and losing them felt like losing his own fingers. That's what attachment does to anyone, with anything.

Kevin Trudeau was walking through the Botanical Gardens in Hawaii with a famous Hollywood artist.

Every few steps she'd stop at a flower. "Kevin, look at this. Isn't it exquisite?" She'd admire it, photograph it, then walk on.

What should have taken 30 minutes took three hours.

She wasn't attached to any of those flowers — she wasn't taking them home. She was just fully enjoying each one while she had it. Kevin says that's exactly how to hold money, things, anything you own.
